lede:
The first time most people write an agent, the system prompt is a constant string. It sits at the top of a file, a few hundred lines long, and every edit means a restart.

Trouble starts with the second agent. The main agent and its subagents need different personas; when a tool gets switched off, the two paragraphs explaining how to use it have to disappear along with it; and the model still needs to know which directory it's in, which model it's running, what the todo list looks like right now — all of which changes every step.

So the constant becomes a template, the template becomes a string-building function, and that function ends up as the place nobody dares touch: you can't say who added any given sentence, or whether something else depends on it if you delete it.

What's worth watching here isn't "how should this prompt be worded."

**It's this: when everyone gets to stuff things into one piece of text, how do you keep the result deterministic, traceable, and loud the moment something goes wrong.**

sections.heading: There is no such thing as "the prompt"
body: Start with a setup that feels a little wrong: nowhere in this thing can you find "the system prompt." There's no variable, no file, no location you can point at and say, there, that's it.
The usual approach is to build the prompt once at startup, keep it, and reuse the same copy on every request. That's reasonable — the prompt doesn't change, so rebuilding it is waste.

This does the opposite: every time the agent loop prepares one step's model request, it asks every contributor again and gets back a four-part result — ordered sections, ordered dynamic context, the list of tools the model can actually see on this step, and a table of variables already resolved down to strings.

The point of recomputing is that every contributor gets asked again. A section's text can be a function, the tool list comes from a function, the variables come from functions too, and all of them get handed the context of who this assembly is for.
So a section can decide what to emit based on who's running right now — including emitting an empty string and making itself disappear entirely. Conditional presence needs no extra machinery.

From there it splits three ways: sections get their variables filled in, get joined into the system prompt, and go out with the request; the tool list rides a different field of the request on the wire; and dynamic context goes into neither, taking a third path — more on that later.

That the tool list and the prompt sections land in the same result is worth a sentence of its own. "Telling the model what it can do" is one thing by design, not two — a prompt and a set of tool descriptions that know nothing about each other.

**Recomputing every step costs something real. What you get back is that "what the model sees on this step" becomes a value you can pass around, validate, and record as a whole — instead of a string thrown together at the moment the request goes out.**

sections.heading: Order shouldn't be a side effect of load order
body: Everyone agrees the order of sentences in a prompt matters. But in practice that order usually falls out of plugin load order, and load order is a product of the dependency graph and the config — change one line of config and it quietly shifts.
Caching makes it worse. Change the prefix and the hit is gone, and the bill goes straight up.
**Which means order isn't just a readability problem. It's a money problem.**

The answer here is to give sections numeric bands. -100 is the framework's own identity statement, fixed; 0 is the persona the deployment writes; 100 through 199 is reserved wholesale for tools, each tool package registering its own usage guidance without consulting the others. The command-line tool takes 105, the persistent terminal 106, web search 110, web fetch 111, language services 112.

Empty sections are dropped at render time. If you want a passage to appear only under some condition, write the text as a function and return an empty string when the condition fails — it simply isn't there.

The tool-runtime section works exactly this way. In code-execution mode the model has to be told there's only one way in, and the text making that claim calls the same check the executor uses when it rejects everything else. Put differently: the prompt cannot announce a rule the registry doesn't enforce.

The tools themselves aren't ordered by bands but by one central list. Unconfigured, they sort by code point — deliberately not a locale-aware comparison, so the result is the same on any machine. Configured, the list must contain exactly one "everything else goes here" placeholder: what you list lands where you listed it, and what you didn't goes into that slot as a block, alphabetically.

Failures are layered: duplicate names or a missing placeholder throw when the config loads; naming a tool nobody ever registered throws at the first assembly; and if some tool provider dares return a tool named the same as the placeholder, assembly fails outright.
**What this chain does is turn order from a side effect of implementation details into a declaration someone has to actually write down.**

sections.heading: Registering carries its own location
body: One process, a main agent and several subagents running at once, different personas, different visible tools. It's the most common requirement and the easiest one to get wrong.

There are two usual approaches: pass a pile of parameters into the assembly function, or just maintain several parallel registries. The first keeps accumulating parameters; the second quickly turns into bickering over which registry a given passage belongs in.

This takes a different line: the act of registering carries its own location. Whichever context you register in is the layer your contribution lands in; register from an agent's own context and only that agent is affected. The key for a layer is the agent object itself, compared by identity.

On read, the global layer goes down first, then same-named entries stack on top along the parent chain, from the most distant ancestor down to the current layer — nearest wins. Variables, sections, and dynamic context all follow this rule. Tool providers are the one exception: they don't override, they accumulate, the global ones plus every layer on the chain contributing together.

A duplicate name within one layer isn't an override, it's a throw. And the error message spells out the right move: if you want per-agent override, register from that agent's context instead. That one sentence saves far more debugging time than it takes to read.

The persona slot makes "override by matching name" concrete: the registry exports the slot name and its band as constants, and the preset package's plugin — the one whose entire job is swapping the persona — imports those same constants to register with. The two names have to literally be the same for the override to take, so it imports a constant rather than retyping the string.
That plugin has an interesting side effect: it can only be mounted inside a scope. Mount it globally and it collides with the registry's own persona registration, and fails on the spot.

**If overriding works by matching names, the name can't be a literal typed out on both sides — otherwise one rename quietly turns "replace" into "both, side by side," an extra passage in the output, and nothing anywhere reports it.**

sections.heading: Let everyone finish editing, then apply it once more
body: Once the initial result is assembled, a waterfall event runs: a chain of listeners each get the same mutable object in turn, each decides whether to hand control further down, and the final return value is the authoritative result. Dispatch is filtered by scope — a listener mounted on one agent only sees that agent's assemblies.
So far this is ordinary extensible design. What's interesting is the two things that come next — both re-applied after the waterfall has finished.
The first is the "complete section." A section can declare that it is the entire system prompt, and once the waterfall ends it's restored as the only section.

So listeners can still adjust tools, context, and variables — those are collaborative — but they can't slip a sentence into a deployment that claims to be the whole thing. More than one effective complete section and the entire assembly fails.

The second is suppression of runtime context. It isn't a boolean switch but a registration that can be taken back: the registry files one itself when the global config turns it off, and the persona plugin in a scope can file one too.

As long as any one suppression is still alive, dynamic context is empty — and it's cleared again after the waterfall, throwing away whatever listeners added. It comes back only when every one of them has been taken back.

Several parties ask for silence for their own reasons, and whoever takes theirs back first shouldn't get to decide for the rest — that's why it isn't a boolean. And suppression only affects the layer that talks to the model; the services that own these facts, and the logic that enforces them, run as usual.

The package also ships a sixty-line companion plugin, mounted on the same waterfall at the highest priority. It waits for everything downstream to finish, takes the final result, and then checks back over it: section names non-empty and non-duplicated, context names likewise, tool names non-empty, variable names valid and their values either a string or nothing at all.
It validates the authoritative result, not the initial one — and that ordering is the whole point of it.

**Open rewriting and the promise "this is the entire prompt" have to hold at the same time. The way to get there isn't restricting who may edit. It's waiting until everyone has finished editing, then applying the non-negotiable part once more.**

sections.heading: Nothing throws when a variable fails to expand
body: Section text can reference variables with double braces. That feature is everywhere; what's worth talking about is its attitude toward failure.
Two usual approaches: substitute an empty string when it can't resolve, or leave the braces exactly as they are. Neither throws, the program keeps running, the request goes out.
The problem is that the recipient of that sentence is a model.

A model isn't going to stop at an unexpanded brace and tell you rendering failed. It just acts on what it reads, literally. The problem surfaces as inexplicably odd behavior, and you have to work backwards from the output to the prompt.
Honestly, I think this is the hardest class of bug in systems like this — no stack, no error, just someone saying "it's being weird today."

The choice here is to throw in all three cases: invalid name, never registered, registered but with no value this time. The error names which section broke and lists every variable currently registered. Better to fail the whole assembly than let one badly rendered sentence out the door.

"Never registered" is judged against whether the table itself holds the name, so a name inherited from the language's prototype chain counts as unknown rather than accidentally resolving to some built-in function. Most days you can't tell the difference; on the day it matters, the difference is large.

The brace edge cases are pinned down too: an opening brace with no closer anywhere after it is emitted as plain text; one that has a closer later but whose own pair is incomplete counts as malformed and throws. Substituted values are not scanned a second time, so a variable whose value happens to contain double braces doesn't expand again.

The cost is that there's no escape syntax right now: if you want a literal pair of double braces, you can't have one. The author lists this among the known limitations, to be revisited when some prompt actually needs it.

**Wherever the consumer downstream is a model rather than code, the failure that doesn't throw is the most expensive kind. So the right posture isn't to get as much of the sentence out as possible. It's to say nothing at all.**

sections.heading: Runtime facts don't belong tacked onto the end
body: Which directory you're in, which model is running, what the todo list looks like now — facts like these change every step, and the model has to know all of them.
Almost every implementation's first instinct is to append them to the end of the system prompt. It's easy, and it does work.

But there's a price, and most people hit it after the fact: "what the model saw at that moment" exists only in the memory of that one request. It isn't in the log, you can't reconstruct it on replay, you don't know how much room it took when compacting, and you can't account for it in an audit.
The approach here is to render those facts as a message in the user role, which — after the pre-step decision — is appended to the session log and from there into the model history.
The repository has one hard rule: anything the model can read must be reconstructable from the session log. This context message is a direct consequence of that rule.

There's a price, of course: one more message in the history, and every step wants to add another. So the loop side keeps a projection that remembers the sequence number and text of the last snapshot still sitting on the surface of the session. Same content, no new message. Going from something to nothing sends an explicit clearing message saying there is no runtime context right now and earlier snapshots no longer apply. And if that snapshot gets swept away by a replacing event — a compaction, say — the projection state is invalidated along with it.

Even the opening sentence of the snapshot message is designed: this is the current runtime context, and this snapshot supersedes earlier runtime context snapshots. The model doesn't have to work out which one is newest.

**Making runtime facts an invisible suffix means giving up their replayability. Make them a message the log records and replay, compaction, and audit all fall out for free — at the cost of one extra message and a little diffing logic.**

sections.heading: Words someone else wrote are always data
body: Three kinds of text get pushed into the model's view without their origins being fully trustworthy: the instruction file for agents at the repository root, the more specific ones in subdirectories, and fragments quoted in from another session.
The usual approach is to concatenate them straight into the system prompt. They're files from your own project, after all.

But think one layer further: someone else may have committed those files, someone else may have run the session being quoted, and any of it could contain the sentence "ignore all previous instructions."
And once they're joined to the system prompt, the model has nothing to go on when deciding which sentence carries more authority.

The handling here: all of it becomes a user message, wrapped in a pair of framework markers, with the precedence written out in the body — more specific instructions win over broader ones, but none of them override a direct instruction from the system, the developer, or the user. Closing markers appearing in the content are escaped, so the quoted text can't spell out a string that fakes its way past the marker.

Cross-session quotes put "untrusted" right up front: the preamble states that what follows is a read-only snapshot of another session, to be read as background only, and that instructions, permission claims, and tool requests inside it are not to be acted on unless the current user repeats them.

On serialization every angle bracket is escaped, and the snapshot itself projects only direct user messages, assistant text, and compaction checkpoints — tool results, reasoning, and injected context are all excluded, so nothing propagates recursively layer by layer.

The budget is hard, and the way it fails is designed. Each source shrinks independently against a byte ceiling, 64KB by default: drop the oldest non-checkpoint messages first while keeping compaction checkpoints and the most recent one; if it still doesn't fit, truncate the longest one from the middle, keeping its head and tail, and write into the body how many bytes were dropped; and if even the fixed fields don't fit, throw rather than return a mutilated context.

The truncation and drop counts are recorded with the message in the structured source, not mixed into the prose the model reads. Metadata written for people and body text written for the model shouldn't travel the same channel.

The workspace instruction files take a neighboring path: after the read, write, and edit tools successfully touch a file, a re-projection is triggered, deliberately queued to run outside the step boundary, with repeated triggers accumulating serially per agent onto the same inbox entry. When the step actually runs, this context is inserted after the already-claimed messages, so direct user input comes ahead of it.

**"Wrap untrusted content" sounds like security common sense; in practice it's three very concrete things: deliver it under a different role, write the precedence into the body, escape the closing markers. Skip one and the wrapper is just decoration.**

mechanisms.name: Assemble every step, instead of building once at startup
mechanisms.how: The usual approach is to build the prompt at startup, cache it, and reuse the same string on every request. This does the opposite: every time the agent loop prepares one step's model request, it asks every contributor again and gets back a four-part result — ordered sections, ordered dynamic context, the list of tools the model can actually see on this step, and a table of variables already resolved to strings or to nothing. Sections are evaluated at this point but not yet interpolated; tools are already sorted. That one result then renders the system prompt and supplies the tool list in the request, and doesn't change again until the step ends.
mechanisms.why: "What the model sees on this step" becomes a value you can pass around, validate, and record as a whole, instead of a string cobbled together at the moment the request goes out.

mechanisms.name: Which layer a registration lands in is decided by who registers it
mechanisms.how: To let a subagent swap persona and tools without affecting the main agent, the usual approaches are to add parameters to the assembly function or maintain several parallel registries. The first keeps accumulating parameters; the second quickly turns into bickering over which registry a given passage belongs in. This takes a different line: the act of registering carries its own location — whichever context you call from is the layer your contribution lands in, and the key for a layer is the agent object itself, compared by identity. On read, the global layer goes down first, then same-named entries stack along the parent chain from the most distant ancestor down to the current layer, and the nearest layer wins. Tool providers are the one exception: they accumulate rather than override. Empty layers are reclaimed automatically, so a long-running process leaves no husks behind.
mechanisms.why: Parameters only ever accumulate, and parallel registries invite arguments over who owns a given passage; bind the location to the caller's own context and both problems disappear at once.

mechanisms.name: Bands order the sections, one list orders the tools
mechanisms.how: The usual approach lets plugins append to the prompt in load order, which makes sequence a side effect of the dependency graph and the config — change one config line and it shifts quietly. Here the two are handled separately. Sections are joined in ascending numeric bands, by convention -100 for the framework identity, 0 for the deployment persona, 100 through 199 for each tool's usage guidance. Tool order runs off one central list: sorted by code point when unconfigured (deliberately not a locale-aware comparison), and when configured the list must contain exactly one "everything else goes here" placeholder — listed tools land where they were listed, unlisted ones go into that slot as a block, alphabetically.
mechanisms.why: Prompt order affects both model behavior and whether the cache prefix hits; it shouldn't be whatever drifted out of implementation details.

mechanisms.name: Once everyone has finished editing, apply it once more
mechanisms.how: The usual extensible approach is to open a rewrite hook, let listeners change what they like, and use whatever comes out. That hook exists here too — a chain of listeners each take the same mutable assembly result, dispatch is filtered by scope, and the final return value is authoritative. But two things are re-applied after the hook has run: if a section declares itself to be the entire system prompt, it is restored as the only section; and if runtime context is suppressed, dynamic context is emptied a second time, discarding whatever listeners added. More than one effective complete section and assembly fails outright.
mechanisms.why: Open rewriting and the promise "this is the entire prompt" have to hold at the same time, and the second one can't be guaranteed by restricting who is allowed to edit.

mechanisms.name: If a variable won't resolve, the whole assembly fails
mechanisms.how: When a template variable won't resolve, the usual approach is to substitute an empty string or leave the braces as they are — neither throws. The problem is that downstream is a model, not code: it won't report an error, it will just act on the literal braces, and the problem surfaces as behavior that's hard to trace back. Here all three cases throw: invalid name, never registered, registered but with no value this time. The error names the section and lists which variables are currently registered. "Registered or not" counts only entries in the table itself, so a name inherited from the language's prototype chain counts as unknown. Substituted values are not scanned a second time.
mechanisms.why: A sentence that failed to render triggers no runtime error at all, yet every step afterwards pays for it.

mechanisms.name: Runtime facts become a message that leaves a trace
mechanisms.how: Facts that change every step — the current directory, the current model — usually get appended to the end of the system prompt. Easy, but then "what the model saw" exists only inside that one request: not in the log, impossible to reconstruct on replay. Here they render as a message in the user role that goes into the session log and from there into the model history. To avoid appending a duplicate every step, the loop side keeps a projection holding the sequence number and text of the last snapshot still on the surface of the session: same content, no new message; going from something to nothing sends an explicit clearing message; and when a replacing event such as a compaction sweeps that snapshot away, the projection state is invalidated with it.
mechanisms.why: Model-visible means reconstructable — that's a hard rule across the whole repository; the diffing projection exists so the rule doesn't cost an extra copy of tokens on every step.

lessons.lesson: Anything the model can read needs a matching record in the log.
lessons.why: Making runtime facts an invisible suffix on the system prompt means "what the model saw" only ever lives inside that one request. Turn them into a message that gets recorded and replay, compaction, and audit all fall out naturally, at the cost of one more message in the history plus a little diffing logic. That trade looks pointless while the system is small; it pays for itself the day something goes wrong.

lessons.lesson: Turn order into an explicit declaration; don't let it be a side effect of load order.
lessons.why: Plugin registration order drifts with the dependency graph and the config, while prompt order both affects model behavior and decides whether the cache prefix hits. One central order table plus an explicit "everything else goes here" placeholder pins down the first few exactly, without forcing a config change every time you add a tool.

lessons.lesson: If a template reference won't resolve, fail the whole assembly — don't blank it, don't pass it through.
lessons.why: The key is that downstream is a model, not code. A badly rendered prompt triggers no runtime error; the model just acts on the literal braces or the missing sentence, and the problem surfaces as behavior with no stack and no error attached. Throwing at assembly time converts that into a definite failure with a section name on it.

lessons.lesson: The rule the prompt announces and the check that enforces it should be the same piece of code.
lessons.why: In code-execution mode, the sentence saying "this is the only way in" calls the same check the executor uses when it rejects everything else. Write the two separately and sooner or later the prompt announces a rule that isn't actually enforced; the model calls accordingly, gets an unknown-tool error, and starts suspecting the whole deployment contradicts itself — after which its behavior is essentially unpredictable.

lessons.lesson: If a mechanism overrides by matching names, that name has to be one shared constant.
lessons.why: Swapping the persona works because the new registration and the one it replaces share a name. If each side hardcodes its own copy of the string, one rename quietly turns "replace" into "both, side by side" — an extra passage in the output, and nothing anywhere reporting it. Export the slot name as a constant, have both sides use it, and that drift becomes impossible at compile time.

tradeoffs: Between two sections in the same band, order comes down to registration order, which is still a product of plugin loading. Determinism therefore rests entirely on the convention that different responsibilities use different bands, with nothing enforcing it. Tool order was normalized; section order wasn't — the author lists this among the known limitations.

Naming a tool in the order table that nobody ever registered fails at the first assembly, not at startup. Only shape problems — duplicate names, missing placeholder — throw when the config loads. This class of config error surfaces one beat late.

There's no escape syntax, so you can't write literal double braces; any complete pair is read as a variable reference. The author's position is to wait until a prompt actually needs it — personally, I find that kind of "not yet" more honest than designing escape rules nobody uses.

Every step reruns every provider: section functions, tool providers, variable providers, all of them. In code-execution mode that section additionally has to be regenerated from the tools visible in the current scope, a cost that grows with the tool count. This is the direct bill for one snapshot per step.

Answering where a given passage of the prompt came from means crossing several plugins: it might be the persona from the config, a preset's override, some tool package's band, or a waterfall listener's rewrite. The assembled result is easy to read; the chain of origins is not.

The byte budget for cross-session quotes is per source, so three sources can each fill their ceiling and the total is three times a single one. And once a snapshot is written into the target session's log it's frozen: later edits, compactions, or deletions in the source session are never reflected — which is both the isolation guarantee and a way for the model to end up reading stale background material.
